Name: Frank Smith
Body: A 19-year-old Western Union messenger who was attacked by a white mob on September 22, 1906. He was stabbed, struck with stones, and thrown from the Forsyth Street bridge in downtown Atlanta. He was buried at South-View Cemetery, where his gravestone still stands.
Source: 1. “Stories from the Soil.” *Fulton County Remembrance Coalition*, https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil.

Name: William Welch
Source: 1. “Stories from the Soil.” *Fulton County Remembrance Coalition*, https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil.

Name: Samuel F. Ware
Body: He was the son of Lessie Lee and the nephew of Atlanta undertaker Lucius L. Lee. In 1916, he arrived in Atlanta, around the same time that his cousin and Lucius's son, Will Lee, had passed away, leaving the Lee undertaker business without any leadership. Not much was known about Samuel's life or business experience outside of the fact that he was a veteran of the Spanish-American War. On the night of Friday, December 8th, police apprehended two men caught digging up a casket from a fresh grave in South-View. Upon interrogation, the men claimed that Samuel Ware had hired them to recover the caskets allegedly for the purpose of reselling them. That same night, police found Samuel transporting two caskets that appeared to have been recently unearthed, followed by more discovered in his undertaking establishment. Samuel Ware and the two men were all arrested, with Ware's bail being set to $10,000. Samuel Ware was later replaced as president of the Atlanta Undertaking Company, with the stockholders disavowing any knowledge or involvement in his crimes. Ware was later convicted and sentenced to 10 years in prison. However, he was granted a new trial by the Georgia Court of Appeals.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 51.

Name: Milton Harvey
Body: Fourteen-year-old Milton Harvey went missing after running an errand on his bicycle in September 1979. His tragic death marked one of the earliest heartbreaks in a terrorizing wave of disappearances that gripped Atlanta's Black community, leaving a grieving city demanding answers for its lost children.
Source: 1. “Composite of the 28 Missing or Murdered Children in the Atlanta Child Murders, circa 1980s.” *Digital Library of Georgia*, Georgia State University Library, https://dlg.usg.edu/record/gsu_ajc_14196.  2. “Atlanta Child Murders Part 18 of 24.” *FBI Vault*, Federal Bureau of Investigation, https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018.

Name: Yusef Bell
Body: Nine-year-old Yusef Bell vanished in October 1979 after walking to a neighborhood store to buy Bruton Snuff for a neighbor. His heartbreaking loss galvanized a community in mourning and galvanized local mothers, including his mother Camille Bell, to form the Committee to Stop Children’s Murders and demand a dedicated task force.
Source: 1. “Composite of the 28 Missing or Murdered Children in the Atlanta Child Murders, circa 1980s.” *Digital Library of Georgia*, Georgia State University Library, https://dlg.usg.edu/record/gsu_ajc_14196.  2. “Atlanta Child Murders Part 18 of 24.” *FBI Vault*, Federal Bureau of Investigation, https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018.

Name: Aaron Wyche
Body: A gentle 10-year-old, Aaron Wyche disappeared in June 1980 after being seen near a local grocery store. His death heightened fear across the city as families realized the mysterious killer was targeting boys of varying ages across metropolitan Atlanta.
Source: 1. “Composite of the 28 Missing or Murdered Children in the Atlanta Child Murders, circa 1980s.” *Digital Library of Georgia*, Georgia State University Library, https://dlg.usg.edu/record/gsu_ajc_14196.  2. “Atlanta Child Murders Part 18 of 24.” *FBI Vault*, Federal Bureau of Investigation, https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018.

Name: Aaron Jackson
Body: Nine-year-old Aaron Jackson disappeared in November 1980, another precious life lost during a terrifying season of fear, driving community leaders and federal investigators to intensify their relentless search for justice.
Source: 1. “Composite of the 28 Missing or Murdered Children in the Atlanta Child Murders, circa 1980s.” *Digital Library of Georgia*, Georgia State University Library, https://dlg.usg.edu/record/gsu_ajc_14196.  2. “Atlanta Child Murders Part 18 of 24.” *FBI Vault*, Federal Bureau of Investigation, https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018.

Name: Patrick Rogers
Body: A vibrant 16-year-old with an infectious spirit, Patrick Rogers was a multi-talented teenager and aspiring musician who lifted spirits by writing music with his friend, Joe Harper. Known affectionately to friends as "Pat Man," he was a familiar, bright face who often hung out near the fast-food restaurant on Moreland Avenue by I-20. When he suddenly vanished in November 1980, the heart-wrenching news echoed through the neighborhood, underscoring the tragic and far-reaching impact of the crisis on Atlanta's youth.
Source: 1. “Composite of the 28 Missing or Murdered Children in the Atlanta Child Murders, circa 1980s.” *Digital Library of Georgia*, Georgia State University Library, https://dlg.usg.edu/record/gsu_ajc_14196.  2. “Atlanta Child Murders Part 18 of 24.” *FBI Vault*, Federal Bureau of Investigation, https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018.

Name: Curtis Walker
Body: Thirteen-year-old Curtis Walker went missing in February 1981 while working odd jobs to help support his family. His death underscored the vulnerability of young boys trying to navigate daily life amidst an unprecedented crisis in their hometown.
Source: 1. “Composite of the 28 Missing or Murdered Children in the Atlanta Child Murders, circa 1980s.” *Digital Library of Georgia*, Georgia State University Library, https://dlg.usg.edu/record/gsu_ajc_14196.  2. “Atlanta Child Murders Part 18 of 24.” *FBI Vault*, Federal Bureau of Investigation, https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018.

Name: William Barrett
Body: Just 17 years old when he disappeared in May 1981, William Barrett's tragic death came during the final months of the harrowing crisis, right as massive local and federal task forces closed in on solving the mysteries behind the disappearances.
Source: 1. “Composite of the 28 Missing or Murdered Children in the Atlanta Child Murders, circa 1980s.” *Digital Library of Georgia*, Georgia State University Library, https://dlg.usg.edu/record/gsu_ajc_14196.  2. “Atlanta Child Murders Part 18 of 24.” *FBI Vault*, Federal Bureau of Investigation, https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018.

Name: John Glover
Body: Breaking historical ground as the first African American to lead an FBI field office, John Glover took the helm during one of the nation's most high-profile investigations. Heading the FBI's involvement with the Atlanta Missing and Murdered Task Force, he navigated intense public pressure and complex cross-agency cooperation to bring federal resources and strategic oversight to the search for answers.
Source: 1. “Serial Killers, Part 5: Wayne Williams and the Atlanta Child Murders.” *Federal Bureau of Investigation*, 7 Feb. 2014, https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/-serial-killers-part-5-wayne-williams-and-the-atlanta-child-murders.

Name: Wayne Williams
Body: An ambitious 23-year-old freelance photographer and music promoter, Wayne Williams became the central figure in the investigation after being spotted near a bridge over the Chattahoochee River. Ultimately convicted in 1982 for the murders of two adult victims, he was identified by law enforcement as the primary suspect in the majority of the child disappearances, bringing a dramatic close to a terrifying period in Atlanta's history when the slayings abruptly stopped following his arrest.
Source: 1. “Serial Killers, Part 5: Wayne Williams and the Atlanta Child Murders.” *Federal Bureau of Investigation*, 7 Feb. 2014, https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/-serial-killers-part-5-wayne-williams-and-the-atlanta-child-murders.

Name: Irene Dobbs Jackson
Body: Dr. Irene Dobbs Jackson (1908–1999), the eldest daughter of John Wesley Dobbs, taught French at Spelman College after earning her master's and doctoral degrees at the University of Toulouse in France (pg. 216). At the time, Black Atlantans could not hold a card at the main branch of the Atlanta Public Library. In March 1959, Spelman history professor Howard Zinn and Atlanta University dean Whitney Young began a federal lawsuit against the library with two plaintiffs, Jackson and Rev. Otis Moss, a Morehouse theology student (pg. 216). The library board agreed to desegregate without a court fight, and in 1959 Jackson became the first African American to receive a card from the main branch (pg. 216). Her daughter Constance recalled threatening phone calls and drive-by harassment in the days that followed (pg. 216). Her son, Maynard Jackson Jr., became Atlanta's first Black mayor (pg. 216). Her epitaph at South-View, from Kahlil Gibran, begins "You have walked among us as a spirit" (pg. 129).
Source: 1. “Auburn Avenue Research Library.” *Building Memories*, Georgia Institute of Technology, https://leading-edge.iac.gatech.edu/building-memories/auburn-avenue-research-library/.  2. Dankowski, Terra, and Carrie Smith. “By the Numbers: Atlanta.” *American Libraries*, 3 Jan. 2017, https://americanlibrariesmagazine.org/2017/01/03/by-the-numbers-atlanta/.

Name: Bishop Henry McNeal Turner
Body:
Born in South Carolina, Henry McNeal Turner moved to Georgia after the Civil War and dedicated himself to planting African Methodist Episcopal congregations across the state. In his view, the church served as the essential foundation for the first schoolhouses, meeting halls, and political training grounds for newly freed people who were not yet fully protected. Beside fellow freedmen, he organized Black men to exercise their newly gained right to vote while encouraging Black women to recognize their political power even without official suffrage, firmly believing that emancipation without active participation was merely another form of control.

Turner witnessed a brief moment when democracy reflected its promises as formerly enslaved men were elected to office, helped draft a new state constitution, and stood in the Georgia Legislature in 1868 as elected representatives. However, Georgia quickly retreated into fear and white supremacy, rewriting laws, expelling Black legislators, and subjecting community leaders to imprisonment, attacks, violence, and exile. Despite his tireless efforts, the Reconstruction era ultimately failed to secure lasting equality, leaving behind a bittersweet legacy of courage in the face of systemic opposition.
Source: 1. Angell, Stephen Ward. “Henry McNeal Turner (1834–1915).” *New Georgia Encyclopedia*, 3 Sept. 2002, https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/arts-culture/henry-mcneal-turner-1834-1915.

Name: Clara A. Howard
Body: Clara A. Howard (1866–1935) enrolled at the Spelman Baptist Seminary in 1881, graduating at the top of its first graduating class in 1887. After teaching in Atlanta for several years, she answered a call from the Women’s Baptist Foreign Missionary Society and moved to Lukunga in the Congo. Joining her Spelman classmate Nora Gordon, who had arrived two years prior, the pair established a school for local children that quickly grew to 100 students, witnessing tremendous growth and development among the young women they taught. However, Howard contracted a severe case of malaria that nearly claimed her life, forcing her to return to Atlanta alongside her most promising student, Flora Zeto Malekebu, who enrolled at Spelman. Though Nora tragically passed away at age 24, Howard survived and lived to age 69; both women, along with Flora, were eventually laid to rest at South-View Cemetery. Howard’s enduring legacy lived on through the Congolese students who followed her path to America and in the naming of Spelman’s Howard-Harreld Hall in her honor.
Source: 1. Historic South-View Preservation Foundation. *Sisters for Eternity: The Spelman College Legacy at South-View Cemetery*. Flyer, 2018.
Picture credit: Clara Howard, 1919. From Clement Richardson, National Cyclopedia of the Colored Race, page 131. Public domain. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ClaraAHoward1919.tif

Name: Casket Scandal
Body:
When Lucius Lee passed away in 1915, his death left a profound vacancy in Atlanta's African American funeral industry. Over a distinguished forty-year career, Lee had built immense community trust through honest dealings and dependable service. His son, Will Lee, who had long partnered in the firm, stepped up to continue his father's legacy, but tragedy struck again when Will passed away in February 1916. Seeking to maintain stability, the family turned to Samuel F. Ware—a Spanish-American War veteran and nephew of Lucius Lee—to take over management of L. L. Lee & Son. Supported by public endorsements from Will's widow, Bessie, and sister, Addie Jackson, Ware managed to rebuild the enterprise on West Mitchell Street after the destructive Great Fire of May 1917, eventually rebranding as the Atlanta Undertaking Company while continuing to leverage the respected Lee family name.

By late 1922, however, unsettling rumors began circulating regarding missing caskets from South-View Cemetery, pointing directly toward Ware. The rumors turned to grim reality on the night of Friday, December 8, when police apprehended two men in the act of exhuming a casket from a fresh grave. Under interrogation, the men confessed that Ware had hired them to unearth caskets for resale. That same night, authorities intercepted Ware carrying two freshly dug caskets and discovered additional stolen caskets at his establishment, leading to his arrest on $10,000 bail. The true horror unfolded the following Monday when distraught families gathered at South-View as police oversaw grave disinterments, only to discover their loved ones had been removed from their caskets and reburied in plain wooden shipping crates.

In the aftermath, South-View issued a public statement of regret, and undertaker David T. Howard was entrusted with the solemn duty of properly reinterring the desecrated bodies, emphasizing in the Atlanta Independent that sacred places must be protected from such trespasses. Stockholders swiftly replaced Ware and disavowed his actions. Though initially convicted and sentenced to 10 years in prison, Ware was granted a new trial by the Georgia Court of Appeals; while condemning his "ghoulish" conduct, the court found that removing a casket while lifting a body was not explicitly covered under Georgia's 1922 criminal code.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 51.

Name: Triple L Movement
Body: In Atlanta, Black riders were made to sit at the back of city buses. In January 1957, soon after the Montgomery Bus Boycott, a group of Black ministers led by Rev. William Holmes Borders of Wheat Street Baptist Church launched the Love, Law, and Liberation (Triple L) Movement to change that. On January 8, Borders told a crowd of more than 1,200 at Wheat Street, "We are going to ride until these buses are desegregated" ("Bus Desegregation in Atlanta"). The next day, six ministers boarded a downtown bus and took the front seats, and police arrested them the following afternoon, creating the test case the ministers had planned for. Two years later, on January 9, 1959, a federal court ruled in their favor, and Atlanta's buses opened to every rider ("Bus Desegregation in Atlanta"). Borders and Rev. Samuel W. Williams, one of the plaintiffs in the bus case, both rest at South-View (pg. 177, 254).
Source:
1. Hatfield, Edward A. "Bus Desegregation in Atlanta." *New Georgia Encyclopedia*, https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/bus-desegregation-in-atlanta/.
2. "From William Holmes Borders." The Martin Luther King, Jr., Research and Education Institute, Stanford University, 6 Apr. 1957, https://kinginstitute.stanford.edu/king-papers/documents/william-holmes-borders.
3. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 177, 254.

Name: Atlanta Student Movement
Body: In 1960, Black Atlantans could shop at downtown stores like Rich's but were refused a seat at their lunch counters and restaurants. That February, students at Atlanta's six historically Black colleges began to organize, and on March 9 they published "An Appeal for Human Rights" in all three of the city's daily newspapers ("Atlanta Sit-ins"). Six days later, nearly 200 students sat in at ten downtown lunch counters, and police arrested 77 of them. On October 19, students returned, this time to Rich's whites-only Magnolia Room, and police arrested more than fifty people, including Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and his brother A.D. King ("Atlanta Sit-ins"). Fred C. Bennette Jr., a Morris Brown student, led the Rich's campaign (pg. 174); Rev. William Holmes Borders chaired the adults who advised the students (pg. 177); and Jesse Hill Jr. helped launch the Atlanta Inquirer as a newspaper of protest (pg. 212). In March 1961 the city's leaders agreed to open the lunch counters, and they did so that October ("Atlanta Sit-ins").
Source:
1. Hatfield, Edward A. "Atlanta Sit-ins." *New Georgia Encyclopedia*, https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/atlanta-sit-ins/.
2. King, Lonnie C., Jr. "Atlanta Student Movement Timeline." Civil Rights Movement Archive, 2013, https://www.crmvet.org/info/60asmtim.htm.
3. "The Atlanta Student Movement." Atlanta History Center, https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/exhibitions/the-color-line-the-problem-of-the-centuries/students-and-strategy/.
4. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 174, 177, 212, 219, 238.

Name: Dr. King Laid to Rest at South-View
Body: On April 9, 1968, five days after he was assassinated in Memphis, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was carried on a mule-drawn farm wagon to South-View Cemetery ("Plan Your Visit"). His burial drew the largest gathering in South-View's history; photographers climbed onto nearby mausoleums to see over the crowd (pg. 114). He was laid to rest in a marble crypt on mausoleum row, its inscription stenciled at first because it was needed so quickly, and an eternal flame and a guard were later added (pg. 69, 115). On what would have been his fortieth birthday, January 15, 1969, about three hundred people gathered at his grave, and thousands more came that year. In January 1970 his body was moved to a tomb near Ebenezer Baptist Church, now part of the King Center (pg. 115). His parents, Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. and Alberta Williams King, were later laid to rest at South-View in the same crypt where their son first rested (pg. 115).
Source:
1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 6, 69, 113–15.
2. "Plan Your Visit." The King Center, https://thekingcenter.org/visit/.
3. "What is South-View Cemetery? Here's the history where John Lewis is buried." WSB-TV, 2020, https://www.wsbtv.com/news/local/atlanta/what-is-south-view-cemetery-heres-history-where-john-lewis-is-buried/CSKPZVG6PFFJXKD3XKCOPKRP2I/.

Name: Hank Aaron's 715th Home Run
Body: Hank Aaron ended the 1973 season one home run short of Babe Ruth's record of 714. That winter he received racist hate mail and threats on his life, and he needed bodyguards and police protection to keep playing ("Watch: Hank Aaron"). His teammates feared someone would shoot him on the field (Odum). On April 8, 1974, in front of a home crowd in Atlanta, he hit his 715th home run off the Dodgers' Al Downing and took the record, and he finished his career with 755 ("Watch: Hank Aaron"). Aaron married Billye Williams, the widow of Rev. Samuel W. Williams (pg. 254). In January 2021 his funeral was held at Friendship Baptist Church, where Rev. Williams had once been pastor, and he was laid to rest at South-View ("Hank Aaron's funeral").
Source:
1. Jaffe, Jay. "Watch: Hank Aaron hits record-breaking 715th homer 40 years ago today." *Sports Illustrated*, 8 Apr. 2014, https://www.si.com/mlb/strike-zone/2014/04/08/video-hank-aaron-715th-homer-40th-anniversary-babe-ruth.
2. Odum, Charles. "Hank Aaron rose above racist hate mail and threats in pursuit of Ruth's home run record 50 years ago." Associated Press, via WABE, 7 Apr. 2024, https://www.wabe.org/hank-aaron-rose-above-racist-hate-mail-and-threats-in-pursuit-of-ruths-home-run-record-50-years-ago/.
3. "Hank Aaron's funeral a tribute to more than a baseball great." *The Atlanta Journal-Constitution*, 28 Jan. 2021, https://ajc.com/sports/hank-aarons-funeral-a-tribute-to-more-than-a-baseball-great/NTMY77KPAFCWFHKNE4LJRBSGS4/.
4. "Hank Aaron laid to rest at permanent gravesite in Atlanta." 11Alive, Jan. 2022, https://11alive.com/article/news/local/hank-aaron-final-resting-place/85-834bd507-a782-4a20-8977-9ab73606cb0b.

Name: The Green Book in Atlanta
Body: Under segregation, a Black family driving through the South could be turned away at a gas station, a restaurant, or a hotel, and some towns were unsafe for them after dark. From 1936 to 1966, Victor Hugo Green, a Harlem postal worker, published the Green Book, a guide to the businesses where Black travelers would be served ("In Segregation-Era Atlanta"). In Atlanta, one of the few gas stations listed was Harden's Service Station on Hunter Street, owned by John and Willie Lee "Billie" Harden, where Black drivers could safely fill up and get repairs ("Atlanta in the Negro Motorist Green Book"). John Harden was the first African American to own and operate a gas station in Atlanta, and the Hardens also owned the Atlanta Black Crackers baseball team (pg. 206). Both rest at South-View.
Source:
1. "Atlanta in the Negro Motorist Green Book." Atlanta History Center, https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/blog/atlanta-in-the-negro-motorist-green-book/.
2. "In Segregation-Era Atlanta, These Places Welcomed Travelers." WABE, https://wabe.org/?p=45670.
3. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 206.

Name: William Holmes Borders
Body: Rev. William Holmes Borders (1905–1993), a third-generation minister, served as pastor of Wheat Street Baptist Church on Auburn Avenue from 1937 until 1988, and the church grew more under his leadership than at any other time in its history (pg. 177). He helped lead early civil rights efforts in Atlanta, including the push to desegregate the Atlanta Police Department in the 1940s and the campaign to desegregate the city's buses in the 1950s (pg. 177). In January 1957 he led the Love, Law, and Liberation (Triple L) Movement, telling a crowd at Wheat Street, "We are going to ride until these buses are desegregated" ("Bus Desegregation in Atlanta"). During the student sit-ins of the 1960s, he chaired the committee of adults who advised the students (pg. 177). In the 1960s and 1970s he led Wheat Street in building low-income housing at Wheat Street Gardens and housing for older residents at Wheat Street Towers, and he used radio and television to build support for civil rights (pg. 178). He rests at South-View.
Source:
1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 177–78.
2. Hatfield, Edward A. "Bus Desegregation in Atlanta." *New Georgia Encyclopedia*, https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/bus-desegregation-in-atlanta/.

Name: Samuel W. Williams
Body: Rev. Samuel Woodrow Williams (1912–1970), an Arkansas native, earned degrees at Morehouse College and Howard University and doctoral degrees at the University of Chicago and Arkansas Baptist College (pg. 254). He was pastor of Friendship Baptist Church from 1954 until his death and chaired the philosophy and religion department at Morehouse College (pg. 254). He served as president of the Atlanta branch of the NAACP, and in 1959 he was one of the plaintiffs in the successful lawsuit that desegregated Atlanta's city buses (pg. 254). He also held leadership roles in the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, the Atlanta Summit Leadership Conference, the Greater Atlanta Council on Human Relations, and the Georgia Council on Human Relations (pg. 254). His widow, Billye Williams, later married baseball player Hank Aaron (pg. 254). He rests at South-View.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 254.

Name: Martin Luther King Sr.
Body: Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. (1899–1984) was pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church for forty-four years (pg. 220). Long before his son became a national leader, he was active in the Atlanta Civic and Political League and the NAACP, led a voting-rights march on Atlanta City Hall in 1936, and pressed for equal pay for Black teachers (pg. 220). He served on the boards of Atlanta University and Morehouse College (pg. 220). His son, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., was first laid to rest at South-View in 1968, and King Sr. and his wife, Alberta Williams King, were later buried in the same crypt where their son had first rested (pg. 115). His epitaph reads "I love Everyone" and "Still in Business, Just Moved Upstairs" (pg. 220).
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 115, 220.

Name: Alberta Williams King
Body: Alberta Williams King (1904–1974). "Her life shall be filled with music," reads her epitaph at South-View (pg. 220). The daughter of Rev. Adam Daniel Williams and Jennie Celeste Parks Williams, she grew up in Ebenezer Baptist Church, where her father was pastor, and she started the church's choir and served as its organist and music director (pg. 220, 254). She attended Spelman Seminary, earned a teaching certificate at Hampton Normal Institute, and taught school before marrying Martin Luther King Sr., who followed her father as pastor of Ebenezer (pg. 220). She was the mother of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. In 1974, a gunman killed her as she played "The Lord's Prayer" during Sunday worship at Ebenezer (pg. 220). She rests at South-View beside her husband (pg. 69, 115).
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 69, 115, 220, 254.

Name: A.D. Williams King
Body: Rev. Alfred Daniel Williams King (1930–1969), the younger brother of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., worked beside his brother in the movement. On October 19, 1960, he was among the more than fifty people arrested in the Atlanta student sit-ins that included Rich's Magnolia Room ("Atlanta Sit-ins"). During the 1963 Birmingham campaign he pastored First Baptist Church of Ensley, also recorded as First Street Baptist Church, and on May 11, 1963, his family's home in Ensley was bombed; the family escaped ("Alabama: A.D. King Home"; pg. 219). In Louisville, Kentucky, where he pastored Zion Baptist Church, he led protests that eventually won an open housing law in Kentucky (pg. 219). He served on the board of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and worked in the Poor People's Campaign, and after his brother's death he became co-pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church with his father (pg. 219). He drowned in the swimming pool at his Atlanta home in 1969; the coroner found no foul play (pg. 219). He rests at South-View.
Source:
1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 219.
2. Hatfield, Edward A. "Atlanta Sit-ins." *New Georgia Encyclopedia*, https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/atlanta-sit-ins/.
3. "Alabama: A.D. King Home." National Park Service, https://www.nps.gov/places/alabama-a-d-king-home.htm.
4. "Birmingham Home of A.D. King Added to Civil Rights Network." *The Atlanta Journal-Constitution*, https://www.ajc.com/news/birmingham-home-of-ad-king-added-to-civil-rights-network/M7PXLQOKKFC75ORBYBQZMIVMAE/.

Name: Fred C. Bennette Jr.
Body: Rev. Fred C. Bennette Jr. (1928–1994) graduated from Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary (pg. 174). While still a student at Morris Brown, he led the sit-in campaign to desegregate Rich's department store (pg. 174). He went on to direct voter registration drives for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC), serve as deputy director of the Georgia Voters League, and become the first director of SCLC's Operation Breadbasket, which organized Black churches to challenge the hiring practices of businesses that would not hire Black workers (pg. 174). He was one of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s closest and most trusted aides, later advised Georgia Governor Jimmy Carter and Atlanta Mayor Andrew Young, and served as security director of the King Center (pg. 174). His gravestone at South-View bears the motto "Commandante," and Andrew Young wrote his epitaph: "You were always there when Martin needed you" (pg. 174).
Source:
1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 174.
2. "Fred C. Bennette, Jr. Collection." Auburn Avenue Research Library on African American Culture and History, finding aid, 2004, https://aspace-gpls.galileo.usg.edu/repositories/3/resources/242.

Name: Ruby Doris Smith-Robinson
Body: Ruby Doris Smith-Robinson (1942–1967) grew up in Atlanta's Summerhill neighborhood and became active in the movement while still a teenager (pg. 238). As a Spelman College student she took part in the sit-ins (pg. 238). After a "jail, no bail" protest in South Carolina, she and other students served thirty days, including time on a chain gang, and during the Freedom Rides she served forty-five days in Mississippi's Parchman Penitentiary (pg. 238). She organized chapters of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) and became the first and only woman to serve as its executive secretary (pg. 238). Her health failed, and she died of cancer at twenty-five (pg. 238). Her epitaph at South-View reads, "If you think free, you are free" (pg. 238).
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 238.

Name: Julian Bond
Body: Julian Bond (1940–2015) became a student protest leader while attending Morehouse College, and in 1960 he helped organize the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC), serving as its first communications director (pg. 177). Atlanta voters elected him to the Georgia House of Representatives in 1965, but in January 1966 the House voted to bar him from his seat because he supported SNCC's statement against the Vietnam War; the U.S. Supreme Court ruled unanimously in December 1966 that the House had violated his right to free speech, and he took his seat (Bond v. Floyd). He later served in the Georgia Senate, co-founded the Southern Poverty Law Center and served as its president, and led the NAACP, first as president of its Atlanta branch and later as chairman of the national organization (pg. 177). He was also a television commentator, newspaper columnist, poet, and college professor (pg. 177). He is remembered at South-View, where a marker carries his epitaph, "Easily Amused Race Man." His parents, educator Horace Mann Bond and librarian Julia Washington Bond, also rest at South-View (pg. 177).
Source:
1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 177.
2. *Bond v. Floyd*, 385 U.S. 116 (1966).

Name: John Lewis
Body: John Lewis (1940–2020) joined the sit-in movement as a college student in Nashville, and in 1961 he rode in the Freedom Rides, where white segregationists attacked him and other riders at the bus station in Montgomery, Alabama (Moye). He moved to Atlanta in 1963 as chair of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) and made the city his home after he left SNCC in 1966 (Moye). In 1965, Alabama state troopers beat Lewis and some 600 marchers as he led them across the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, on the day remembered as "Bloody Sunday" (Moye). He won an at-large seat on the Atlanta City Council in 1981 and then represented Georgia's Fifth Congressional District in the U.S. House for more than thirty years (Moye). He died on July 17, 2020, and on July 30 he was laid to rest at South-View beside his wife, Lillian Miles Lewis, a librarian at Atlanta University who was his chief adviser in his successful campaign for Congress ("John Lewis: A Founding Father"; pg. 223).
Source:
1. Moye, J. T. "John Lewis (1940–2020)." *New Georgia Encyclopedia*, 20 July 2020, https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/government-politics/john-lewis-1940-2020/.
2. "John Lewis: A Founding Father of a better America." *The Atlanta Journal-Constitution*, 30 July 2020, https://www.ajc.com/john-lewis/john-lewis-a-founding-father-of-a-better-america/2PYQEPHYIRH7NE4R6B5SS2JPZU/.
3. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 223.

Name: Jesse Hill Jr.
Body: Jesse Hill Jr. (1926–2012) earned an MBA in actuarial science at the University of Michigan and became the third president of Atlanta Life Insurance Company, the company Alonzo Herndon founded (pg. 210–11). In the summer of 1960 he helped launch the Atlanta Inquirer newspaper "as a voice of protest against racial discrimination" and as an outlet for positive coverage of the movement (pg. 212). Though he never held political office, he advised Atlanta mayors from Sam Massell to Kasim Reed, as well as Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and Governor Jimmy Carter, and he was known for building alliances between Black and white leaders (pg. 211). He became the first Black president of the Metro Atlanta Chamber of Commerce, the first Black member and later chair of the Board of Regents of Georgia's university system, and chair of the King Center's board (pg. 212). Part of Butler Street now carries his name (pg. 212). He rests at South-View (pg. 6).
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 6, 210–12.

Name: Herman J. Russell
Body: Herman Jerome Russell (1930–2014) was born in Atlanta during the Great Depression and began shining shoes and selling Coca-Colas as a child; by sixteen he had saved $125 to buy his first piece of property, and the rent from it paid for his college education (pg. 239). After earning a degree in construction at Tuskegee, he built H. J. Russell and Company, which helped build much of Atlanta's skyline (pg. 239). During the height of the movement he paid bail bonds for jailed activists and was a major donor to the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (pg. 239). He was the first Black member of the Metro Atlanta Chamber of Commerce and its second Black president, after his close friend Jesse Hill Jr. (pg. 239). He rests at South-View (pg. 6).
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 6, 239.

Name: Jesse B. Blayton Sr.
Body: Jesse Bee Blayton Sr. (1897–1977), a World War I veteran, became the first Black certified public accountant in Georgia in 1928 (pg. 175). He taught accounting and economics at Morehouse College, Atlanta University, and Morris Brown College, co-founded the Mutual Federal Savings and Loan Association, which made home loans to Black families, and served as cashier and vice president of Citizens Trust Bank (pg. 175). In 1949 he bought WERD, the first radio station in the United States owned by African Americans; his son, J. B. Blayton Jr., managed the station for twenty years (pg. 175–76). With Clayton Yates and Lorimer Milton he also owned the Top Hat Club on Auburn Avenue (pg. 192). He was inducted into the Radio Hall of Fame in 1995 (pg. 175). He rests at South-View.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 175–76, 192.

Name: John and Billie Harden
Body: John Harden (d. 1979) and Willie Lee "Billie" Harden (d. 1991). John Harden was the first African American to own and operate a gas station in Atlanta (pg. 206). He opened the Harden Service Station on Hunter Street around 1930 and bought a second station on Auburn Avenue in 1935, and he kept it open twenty-four hours a day, closing only once in thirty years, on the day President John F. Kennedy was assassinated (pg. 206). Harden's was one of the few stations in Atlanta listed in the Green Book where Black travelers could safely buy gas and get repairs ("Atlanta in the Negro Motorist Green Book"). John and Billie Harden also co-owned and managed the Atlanta Black Crackers baseball team, which they bought in 1937 (pg. 206; "Atlanta in the Negro Motorist Green Book"). Both rest at South-View, where their mausoleum carries the family name.
Source:
1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 206.
2. "Atlanta in the Negro Motorist Green Book." Atlanta History Center, https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/blog/atlanta-in-the-negro-motorist-green-book/.
3. Historic South-View Preservation Foundation. *South-View Would Like to Welcome Georgia Tech for a Historic Tour*. Tour handout, 3 June 2026.

Name: Hank Aaron
Body: Henry "Hank" Aaron (1934–2021) ended the 1973 season one home run short of Babe Ruth's record and spent that winter receiving racist hate mail and threats, needing bodyguards and police protection to keep playing ("Watch: Hank Aaron"). On April 8, 1974, in Atlanta, he hit his 715th home run off the Dodgers' Al Downing and took the record ("Watch: Hank Aaron"). He married Billye Williams, the widow of Rev. Samuel W. Williams (pg. 254). After his death in January 2021, his funeral was held at Friendship Baptist Church, Rev. Williams's former church, and he was laid to rest at South-View ("Hank Aaron's funeral"; pg. 254).
Source:
1. Jaffe, Jay. "Watch: Hank Aaron hits record-breaking 715th homer 40 years ago today." *Sports Illustrated*, 8 Apr. 2014, https://www.si.com/mlb/strike-zone/2014/04/08/video-hank-aaron-715th-homer-40th-anniversary-babe-ruth.
2. "Hank Aaron's funeral a tribute to more than a baseball great." *The Atlanta Journal-Constitution*, 28 Jan. 2021, https://ajc.com/sports/hank-aarons-funeral-a-tribute-to-more-than-a-baseball-great/NTMY77KPAFCWFHKNE4LJRBSGS4/.
3. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 254.

Name: Atlanta's First Black Police Officers
Body: Atlanta hired its first Black police officers in 1948, after pressure from Black civic leaders, including Rev. William Holmes Borders of Wheat Street Baptist Church (pg. 177). Eight men joined the force that spring: Henry Hooks, Claude Dixon, Ernest H. Lyons, Robert McKibbens, Willard Strickland, Willie T. Elkins, Johnnie P. Jones, and John Sanders ("Tracing the Atlanta 8"). About four hundred people turned out to watch their first patrol on April 3, 1948 ("Tracing the Atlanta 8"). The eight were not allowed in police headquarters, so they worked out of the basement of the Butler Street YMCA. They could not wear their uniforms to and from work or drive squad cars, and they walked their beats in Black neighborhoods (pg. 242). If they stopped a white suspect, they had to call a white officer, and they could not arrest white people until 1962 ("Tracing the Atlanta 8"). Willard Strickland, one of the eight, rests at South-View (pg. 242–43).
Source:
1. "Tracing the Atlanta 8 through Sweet Auburn." Atlanta History Center, https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/blog/tracing-the-atlanta-8-through-sweet-auburn/.
2. "Black in Blue: Atlanta's First African American Police Officers." *Atlanta*, https://www.atlantamagazine.com/great-reads/black-blue-atlantas-first-african-american-police-officers-vanguards-civil-rights-movement/.
3. "Willard L. Strickland Papers." Auburn Avenue Research Library on African American Culture and History, finding aid, https://aafa.galileo.usg.edu/repositories/2/resources/25.
4. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 177, 242–43.

Name: Southern Christian Leadership Conference Founded
Body: In January 1957, soon after the Montgomery Bus Boycott, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and other leaders called about sixty Black ministers and activists to Atlanta to carry the boycott's nonviolent methods across the South ("This Far by Faith"). They met at Ebenezer Baptist Church, where King's father was pastor ("Reasons to Celebrate Black History Month: SCLC"; pg. 220). Later that year the group took the name Southern Christian Leadership Conference, with King as its first president, and it set out to end segregation through nonviolent direct action ("Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC)"; "Martin Luther King Jr. Fast Facts"). Its first headquarters was on Auburn Avenue in the Prince Hall Masonic Temple, which the Masons had built under the leadership of John Wesley Dobbs (pg. 100; "Prince Hall Masonic Temple"). Several South-View residents helped carry its work: Rev. Samuel W. Williams held leadership roles in the SCLC, Rev. A.D. King served on its board, Rev. Fred C. Bennette Jr. directed its voter registration drives and was the first director of its Operation Breadbasket, and Herman J. Russell was a major donor (pg. 174, 219, 239, 254).

Name: Atlanta Public Library Desegregated
Body: For decades, Black Atlantans could not borrow books from the city's main library and could read there only in the basement ("The Woman Who Desegregated Atlanta's Library System"). They were served instead at separate branches, such as the Auburn Avenue Branch, whose first librarian in 1921 was Alice Dugged Cary, and the West Hunter Branch, managed from 1949 by Annie L. McPheeters (pg. 187, 228). In March 1959, Spelman history professor Howard Zinn and Atlanta University dean Whitney Young began a federal lawsuit against the library with two plaintiffs, Spelman professor Dr. Irene Dobbs Jackson and Rev. Otis Moss, a Morehouse theology student (pg. 216). Rather than fight in court, the library board agreed to desegregate. Jackson became the first African American to receive a card from the main branch, and music professor Earl A. Sanders received his at the same time (pg. 216). Jackson's daughter Constance later recalled threatening phone calls and drive-by harassment in the days that followed (pg. 216). In 1976, Ella Gaines Yates became the first African American director of the Atlanta-Fulton Public Library system (pg. 258). Jackson, Cary, McPheeters, and Yates all rest at South-View.

Name: Atlanta Schools and UGA Desegregated
Body: Seven years after the Supreme Court's 1954 ruling in Brown v. Board of Education, Georgia's schools and colleges were still segregated. Dr. Horace Mann Bond, who later led Atlanta University's school of education, had helped research the Brown case for the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund (pg. 177). In 1961, the barriers began to fall. After a two-year legal fight by the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund and Atlanta lawyers Donald Hollowell, Vernon Jordan, and Horace Ward, federal judge William Bootle ordered the University of Georgia on January 6 to admit Hamilton Holmes and Charlayne Hunter ("Charlayne Hunter-Gault"). Jesse Hill Jr. had met the two Turner High School graduates in 1959 and helped them look for a white Georgia college to desegregate ("Hamilton Holmes"). When they arrived to register on January 9, they were met with taunts and slurs. Two days later, after a basketball game, a crowd gathered outside Hunter's dormitory and smashed windows, and the university suspended both students until a new court order returned them to class ("Charlayne Hunter-Gault"; "Ernest Vandiver"). That August, after an NAACP lawsuit first filed in 1958, nine Black students entered four all-white Atlanta high schools, Brown, Grady, Murphy, and Northside, on August 30, 1961 ("NAACP and School Desegregation"). Remembered as the Atlanta Nine, they were Madelyn Nix, Thomas Welch, Willie Jean Black, Arthur Simmons, Donita Gaines, Lawrence Jefferson, Mary McMullen, Martha Ann Holmes, and Rosalyn Walton ("Photos: How Atlanta Public Schools Integrated"). Hill and Bond rest at South-View.

Name: Peyton Road Wall
Body: In December 1962, Dr. Clinton Warner, a Black surgeon, bought a home in Peyton Forest, a white section of Cascade Heights in southwest Atlanta ("Atlanta's Berlin Wall"). White homeowners asked the city to keep more Black families out, and on December 17 the Board of Aldermen approved their plan. Mayor Ivan Allen Jr. then had barricades built across Peyton Road and Harlan Road, cutting the white streets off from the Black neighborhood next to them ("Atlanta's Berlin Wall"; "Atlanta's 'Berlin Wall'"). Black Atlantans called it "Atlanta's Berlin Wall" ("Atlanta's 'Berlin Wall'"). Attorney Donald Hollowell took the city to court, and on March 1, 1963, Judge George P. Whitman ruled the barricades unconstitutional; the mayor had them torn down within minutes ("Civil Rights Giant"; "Atlanta's 'Berlin Wall'"). The wall stood for less than three months. Historian Ronald Bayor writes that Allen allowed it as part of an effort to keep the neighborhood white ("Ivan Allen Jr. Biography: Peyton Road Wall").

Name: The Civil Rights Act Tested in Atlanta
Body: On July 2, 1964, President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act, which barred businesses open to the public from turning people away because of their race ("Pickrick Showdown"). The next day, three Black ministry students at Atlanta's Interdenominational Theological Center, George Willis, Albert Dunn, and Woodrow T. Lewis, drove to Lester Maddox's Pickrick restaurant to be served. Maddox met them with a pistol and called on his customers to grab the ax handles he kept by the door, and the three were driven off ("Pickrick Showdown"; "Atlanta Restaurant Suit to Test New Rights Act"). On July 4, Moreton Rolleston's Heart of Atlanta Motel turned away two more Black ministers ("Heart of Atlanta Motel Incident"). The NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund sued Maddox ("Atlanta Restaurant Suit"), and Rolleston sued to overturn the law. On December 14, 1964, a unanimous Supreme Court upheld the law in Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States ("Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States 1964"). T.M. Alexander Sr., an Atlanta insurance leader whom President Johnson appointed to a national citizens' committee to help put the new law into practice, rests at South-View (pg. 170).

Name: Grady Hospital Desegregated
Body: Grady Memorial Hospital opened in 1892 in the heart of Black Atlanta, but for more than seventy years it kept Black and white patients in separate and unequal facilities, so that Atlantans called it "the Gradies" (Lovasik et al.; "Grady Health System"). Even the "New Grady" that opened in 1958 split patients by race, wing by wing (Lovasik et al.). In 1962, Atlanta dentist Dr. Roy C. Bell sued in federal court, joined by seven other Black medical professionals, applicants turned away from Grady's nursing school, and three Black citizens who had been denied emergency treatment ("Timeline of Major Events"; "Roy Charles Bell"). On June 1, 1965, a quiet memo from superintendent Bill Pinkston announced, "All phases of the hospital are on a non-racial basis, effective today" (Lovasik et al.). That same year Grady's two nursing schools were combined, ending the separate school for Black nurses that Ludie Clay Andrews had organized in 1914 (pg. 171). Andrews rests at South-View, as do Eula Benning, a Grady-trained nurse, and Dr. Asa G. Yancey Sr., who in 1958 became the first Black doctor at Grady and in 1972 its medical director (pg. 171, 174, 257–58).

4. "Roy Charles Bell, Pioneering Dentist and Civil Rights Leader." *The Atlanta Journal-Constitution*, https://ajc.com/news/local/roy-charles-bell-pioneering-dentist-and-civil-rights-leader/QJGlfs0QHKcbSa1nIQyoVN.

Name: Summerhill Uprising
Body: On September 6, 1966, Atlanta police shot Harold Prather, a 25-year-old Black man, as they tried to arrest him in the Summerhill neighborhood ("The Summerhill Riot or the Atlanta Rebellion?"; "The Truth"). Hundreds of residents gathered to protest. Mayor Ivan Allen Jr. came to Summerhill and climbed onto a police car to urge the crowd to go home, but he was heckled and knocked off the car (Ivan Allen Digital Collection). Allen blamed the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC); police raided SNCC's office, and its chairman, Stokely Carmichael, was convicted of inciting a riot (Ivan Allen Digital Collection). SNCC said none of its members were there when the crowd first gathered ("The Truth"). Allen called it a riot. Many Black Atlantans saw an uprising against police violence and the deep inequity of the "City Too Busy to Hate," and it is also remembered as the Atlanta Rebellion ("The Summerhill Riot or the Atlanta Rebellion?"). Ruby Doris Smith-Robinson, a SNCC leader, grew up in Summerhill, and Charles Walter "Pete" Greenlea co-founded Summerhill Neighborhood Inc., a community development corporation; both rest at South-View (pg. 203, 238).

Name: Martin Luther King Jr.
Body: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. (1929–1968) was born in Atlanta on January 15, 1929, the son of Rev. Martin Luther King Sr. and Alberta Williams King, and grew up in Ebenezer Baptist Church, where his grandfather and then his father were pastor ("Martin Luther King Jr. – Biographical"; pg. 220, 254). He graduated from Morehouse College in 1948 and earned his doctorate at Boston University in 1955 ("Martin Luther King Jr. – Biographical"). As a young pastor in Montgomery, Alabama, he led the bus boycott that began in December 1955, and in 1957 he became the first president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference ("Martin Luther King Jr. – Biographical"; "Martin Luther King Jr. Fast Facts"). In 1960 he came home to Atlanta as co-pastor of Ebenezer with his father, and that October he was arrested with students at the Rich's sit-in ("Martin Luther King Jr. Fast Facts"; "Atlanta Sit-ins"). In 1964, at thirty-five, he received the Nobel Peace Prize ("Martin Luther King Jr. – Biographical"). On April 4, 1968, he was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee, where he had gone to support striking sanitation workers ("Martin Luther King Jr. – Biographical"). Five days later he was laid to rest at South-View, and in January 1970 his body was moved to a tomb near Ebenezer, now part of the King Center (pg. 114–15). His epitaph reads, "Free at last, Free at last, Thank God Almighty, I'm Free at last" (pg. 165).

2. "Martin Luther King Jr. Fast Facts." CNN, via KEYT, 7 Jan. 2026, https://keyt.com/news/national-world/cnn-national/2026/01/07/martin-luther-king-jr-fast-facts/.

Name: Grace Towns Hamilton
Body: Grace Towns Hamilton (1907–1992), the daughter of Atlanta University professor George A. Towns and Nellie McNair Towns, graduated from Atlanta University, earned a master's degree at Ohio State University, and taught psychology at Clark College, Atlanta University, and LeMoyne Junior College in Memphis (pg. 204–5, 245). In 1943 she became the first woman to serve as executive director of the Atlanta Urban League (pg. 204). In a June 1965 special election, she and seven Black men won seats in the Georgia House of Representatives, the first Black members of the House since Reconstruction, and she became the first Black woman in the Georgia General Assembly (Spritzer and Bergmark). She served in the House until 1985 and was a principal architect of the 1973 Atlanta city charter, which brought Black Atlantans onto the City Council in proportion to their share of the population (Spritzer and Bergmark; pg. 205). She later advised the U.S. Civil Rights Commission, and in 2006 she was named a Georgia Woman of Achievement (pg. 205). She rests at South-View.
Source:
1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 204–5, 245.
2. Spritzer, Lorraine Nelson, and Jean B. Bergmark. "Grace Towns Hamilton (1907–1992)." *New Georgia Encyclopedia*, https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/grace-towns-hamilton-1907-1992/.

Name: Willard L. Strickland
Body: Willard L. Strickland (1922–1989) was born in Atlanta on August 19, 1922, attended Morehouse College, and served in the Army during World War II (pg. 243; "Willard L. Strickland Papers"). In 1948 he was one of the eight Black men who desegregated the Atlanta Police Department (pg. 242). The eight used the Butler Street YMCA as their precinct, could not wear their uniforms to and from work, patrolled Black neighborhoods on foot, and were not allowed to drive squad cars or arrest white people (pg. 242). Strickland left the Atlanta force in 1961, and in 1964 he joined the Decatur Police Department and helped integrate it ("Willard L. Strickland Papers"; pg. 243). He later worked twenty-two years for the U.S. Postal Service in Manhattan, and he received the Atlanta NAACP Honor Award and the Postal Service's Outstanding Service Award (pg. 243). He died on November 1, 1989, and rests at South-View.
Source:
1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 242–43.
2. "Willard L. Strickland Papers." Auburn Avenue Research Library on African American Culture and History, finding aid, https://aafa.galileo.usg.edu/repositories/2/resources/25.

Name: Q.V. Williamson Sr.
Body: Quentin V. Williamson Sr. (1918–1985) was born in Atlanta on December 25, 1918, graduated from Morehouse College, and built one of the largest Black-owned real estate firms in the South (pg. 254–55; "Q. V. Williamson and Morris Finley"). Shut out of the white realtors' association, Black real estate agents in Atlanta formed the Empire Real Estate Board in 1939; Williamson served as its president and as president and chairman of the National Association of Real Estate Brokers (pg. 255, 275). In 1965, Atlanta voters elected him to the Board of Aldermen, now the City Council, making him its first Black member since Reconstruction (pg. 254; "1965 Atlanta Board of Aldermen Election"). His leadership on the council, in the Atlanta Negro Voters League, and in other civic groups helped open public and private housing in Atlanta to Black families (pg. 255). "A free man's dream is to own his own home, in the place of his choice," he said (pg. 255). He rests at South-View.
Source:
1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 254–55, 275.
2. "Q. V. Williamson and Morris Finley." Atlanta History Center, via Digital Library of Georgia, https://dlg.usg.edu/record/geh_byd_939.
3. "1965 Atlanta Board of Aldermen Election." Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_Atlanta_Board_of_Aldermen_election.

Name: Rheubin M. Taylor
Body: Rheubin Marcellus Taylor (d. 1991) taught science and math in the Atlanta Public Schools and served as president of the Georgia Teachers and Education Association, the state's association of Black teachers (pg. 218, 243). At a time when Atlanta paid Black teachers less than white teachers, he and the Atlanta NAACP sued the board of education for equal pay, and NAACP lawyer Constance Baker Motley, later a federal judge, represented the teachers (pg. 243; Davis v. Cook). The school system then fired him, saying the reason was not the lawsuit but an absence without leave while he attended his graduate school reunion; the board overturned the firing on appeal but moved him to an elementary school, and he resigned soon after (pg. 243–44). He went on to work seventeen years as a conciliations supervisor for the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (pg. 244). He rests at South-View.
Source:
1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 218, 243–44.
2. *Davis v. Cook*, 80 F. Supp. 443 (N.D. Ga. 1948), https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/FSupp/80/443/1869187/.

Name: Roscoe E. Thomas Jr.
Body: Roscoe Edwin Thomas Jr. (d. 1996) graduated from Morehouse College and from the University of Michigan Law School in 1947 (pg. 244). In 1951, Dr. Hamilton M. Holmes, his sons Alfred "Tup" and Oliver Holmes, and Charles Bell were turned away from the city-owned Bobby Jones Golf Course because they were Black ("The Legal Case"). In 1953, with only a few years of experience, Thomas served as lead counsel in Holmes v. Atlanta, the first desegregation lawsuit tried in the city (pg. 244). The case reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which ruled on November 7, 1955, and that Christmas Eve and Christmas Day Black golfers played Atlanta's public courses for the first time ("About the Exhibit"; pg. 244). Thomas was a founding member and third president of the Gate City Bar Association and served as general counsel for Citizens Trust Bank, Atlanta Life Insurance Company, and Mutual Federal Savings and Loan (pg. 244). He rests at South-View.
Source:
1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 244.
2. "The Legal Case." *Holmes v. Atlanta: Changing the Game*, Georgia Institute of Technology, https://sites.gatech.edu/holmesvatlanta/legalcase.
3. "About the Exhibit." *Holmes v. Atlanta: Changing the Game*, Georgia Institute of Technology, https://sites.gatech.edu/holmesvatlanta/about-the-case.

Name: T.M. Alexander Sr.
Body: Theodore Martin "T.M." Alexander Sr. (1909–2001) was born in Montgomery, Alabama, on March 7, 1909, graduated from Morehouse College, and founded Alexander & Company, one of the nation's most successful Black-owned insurance agencies, whose clients included Coca-Cola, the City of Atlanta, and Fulton County (pg. 170; "T.M. Alexander, Sr. Papers"). During the Montgomery Bus Boycott, when insurance companies canceled coverage on the church station wagons that carried boycotters to work, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. turned to Alexander, who arranged insurance through Lloyd's of London so the carpools could keep running (pg. 170; "Clarence L. Jordan"). A friend of King, he served as president of the Atlanta branch of the NAACP and of the Empire Real Estate Board (pg. 170). After the Civil Rights Act of 1964, President Lyndon Johnson appointed him to a national citizens' committee to help put the new law into practice (pg. 170). He rests at South-View.
Source:
1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 170.
2. "T.M. Alexander, Sr. Papers." Auburn Avenue Research Library on African American Culture and History, finding aid, https://aafa.galileo.usg.edu/repositories/2/resources/6.
3. "Clarence L. Jordan." The Martin Luther King, Jr., Research and Education Institute, Stanford University, https://kinginstitute.stanford.edu/king-papers/documents/clarence-l-jordan.

Name: Frederick and Bennie McLendon
Body: Dr. Frederick Earl McLendon (d. 1981) and Bennie Bell McLendon (d. 1995). Dr. McLendon, a native of Washington, Georgia, and a graduate of Meharry Medical College, opened the McLendon Medical Clinic for Black Atlantans in 1946; by the time the hospital closed in 1981, more than fifty Black and four hundred white doctors had trained there (pg. 227). Jet magazine called him a "militant medic" (pg. 227). As president of the Atlanta Medical Association, the city's association of Black doctors, he wired Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. to offer doctors and medical aid to victims of police brutality in Selma, joined other doctors in demonstrations for equal pay for African Americans, and was arrested with other doctors at a medical conference when they tried to eat lunch in the segregated cafeteria of Atlanta's Biltmore Hotel (pg. 227, 231). Bennie Bell McLendon, a Fisk University graduate whom her husband called the "brain power" behind the hospital, served as its secretary for thirty-five years and led the women's auxiliaries of the Atlanta Medical Association, the Georgia State Medical Association, and the National Medical Association (pg. 228). She was co-founder and first president of the Atlanta chapter of The Links, and with Dorothy Alexander she led the protest to desegregate the Metropolitan Opera's annual Atlanta performances at the Fox Theatre (pg. 170, 228). Both rest at South-View.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 170, 227–28, 231.

Name: Asa G. Yancey Sr.
Body: Dr. Asa Greenwood Yancey Sr. (1916–2013) was born in Atlanta on August 19, 1916, the son of mail carrier Arthur H. Yancey and Daisy Sherard Yancey, who led the Neighborhood Union from 1950 until it disbanded in 1962 (pg. 257; "A Long and Distinguished Career"). He graduated from Morehouse College and the University of Michigan Medical School, studied under Dr. Charles R. Drew at Freedmen's Hospital in Washington, D.C., and spent ten years as chief of surgery at the Tuskegee Veterans Hospital (pg. 257). In 1958 he came home to Grady Memorial Hospital as chief of surgery at its Hughes Spalding Pavilion, becoming the first Black doctor at Grady, and he became the first Black faculty member of Emory University's medical school (pg. 257). At Emory he started the first accredited surgical training program for Black doctors in Georgia, and in 1972 he became medical director of Grady and an associate dean of Emory's medical school (pg. 257–58). He also served on the Atlanta Board of Education (pg. 258). He rests at South-View.
Source:
1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 257–58.
2. "A Long and Distinguished Career." Department of Surgery, Emory University School of Medicine, https://med.emory.edu/departments/surgery/education/general-surgery-residency/asa-yancey-bio.html.
3. "Asa G. and Carolyn D. Yancey Papers." Atlanta History Center, finding aid, https://ahc.galileo.usg.edu/repositories/2/resources/3187.

Name: Eula Benning
Body: Eula Benning (d. 1964) graduated from the Grady School of Nursing and earned a bachelor of science in nursing education at New York University (pg. 174). She supervised public health nurses for Atlanta and Fulton County and served on the executive committee of the National Nursing Association (pg. 174). She worked for the education and professional recognition of Black nurses: in 1963 she founded the Atlanta School for Practical Nurse Education, and as the last president of Georgia's association of Black nurses she helped bring it into the state's association of white nurses (pg. 174). At her funeral in 1964, practical nurses who had graduated from her school only two weeks before served as flower ladies (pg. 174). The Atlanta chapter of the Grady Nurses Conclave, the Eula Benning Club, is named in her honor (pg. 174). She rests at South-View.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 174.

Name: John H. Calhoun Jr.
Body: John Henry Calhoun Jr. (1899–1988) earned his college degree from Morehouse College at thirty-eight and a master's degree from Atlanta University at sixty-nine (pg. 185). He co-founded the Atlanta Negro Voters League, chaired the Atlanta NAACP's Legal Redress Committee, and in 1956 became president of the Atlanta branch of the NAACP (pg. 185; "John H. Calhoun, Jr. Papers"). When a court ordered him to turn over the branch's records, he refused and went to jail for contempt (pg. 185; "John H. Calhoun, Jr. Papers"). During the sit-ins he worked with the students to desegregate Atlanta's lunch counters and stores ("John H. Calhoun, Jr. Papers"). In 1973, at seventy-four, he was elected to the Atlanta City Council, where he introduced the resolution that created the city's Neighborhood Planning Units, which give residents a voice in city planning (pg. 185; "John H. Calhoun, Jr. Papers"). He rests at South-View.
Source:
1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 185.
2. "John H. Calhoun, Jr. Papers." Robert W. Woodruff Library, Atlanta University Center, finding aid, https://findingaids.auctr.edu/repositories/2/resources/91.

Name: Virgil W. Hodges
Body: Virgil Wendell Hodges (d. 1985) was a sociology professor and department chair at Clark College, later dean of Albany State College, and city editor of the Atlanta Daily World (pg. 212). In the 1940s he chaired the administrative board of the Atlanta chapter of the NAACP, and when a judge ordered him to turn over a list of the chapter's members, he refused (pg. 212). Decades later, in the 1980s, he was the most prolific membership chairman in the chapter's history (pg. 213). His wife, Ruth Hall Hodges, chaired the art department at Morris Brown College and was the first Black woman in Atlanta to own a photography studio (pg. 213). He rests at South-View.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 212–13.

Name: Horace Mann Bond
Body: Dr. Horace Mann Bond (1904–1972), a historian and educator, was born in Nashville, Tennessee, on November 8, 1904 (pg. 177; "Horace Mann Bond"). He was the first president of Fort Valley State College, from 1939 to 1945, and the first Black president of Lincoln University, his alma mater, from 1945 to 1957 (pg. 177; "Horace Mann Bond"). With historians C. Vann Woodward and John Hope Franklin, he did research for the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund in Brown v. Board of Education (pg. 177). From 1957 until shortly before his death he was dean of the school of education at Atlanta University (pg. 177). His wife, Julia Washington Bond, earned her master's degree in library science at fifty-six and worked as a librarian at Atlanta University and the Robert W. Woodruff Library until she retired at ninety-two, and their son, Julian Bond, helped organize SNCC (pg. 177). He died in Atlanta on December 21, 1972, and rests at South-View (pg. 177).
Source:
1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 177.
2. "Horace Mann Bond." *New Georgia Encyclopedia*, https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/education/horace-mann-bond-1904-1972/.
